newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Southeast Asian, Indian food firms poised for boom.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian, Indian food firms poised for boom.

text.p: Food companies are poised for phenomenal growth as the peoples of Southeast Asia and India sharply increase their consumption in line with rising incomes and population, government and bank officials said on Wednesday.

"The Southeast Asian food and agribusiness market is expected to grow tremendously as the region's population surges from 450 million currently to 615 million (people) by the year 2010," Philip Yeo, chairman of Singapore's Economic Development Board, said on the last day of an Agribusiness conference here.

The region's food market, which was worth US$19 billion in 1992, will probably triple in worth to $60 billion by then, Yeo added. Growth rates in Southeast Asia's food industry ranges between 5.0-12.0 percent against 0-3.0 percent growth in the U.S. and the EU.
"The figures we have seen this morning are mind-boggling," Henk Visser, a member of the Executive Board of Dutch cooperative Rabobank, told reporters in a briefing.

Wee Chow Hou, dean of the faculty of business administration in the National University of Singapore (NUS), said a study of a survey carried out by the university showed that major agribusiness corporations are gearing up for business expansion.
"As Asia develops from low income to high income (economies), the first thing people will spend on is higher quality food before they move onto consumer items," Wee said.

The only difference to be noted among food companies in Southeast Asia and in India would be in the form expansion will take, a summary of the study by Wee and Tsui Kai Chong, deputy director of the Graduate School of Business in the NUS, said.

Indian and Indonesian executives would prefer to enlarge existing facilities. Thai and Singaporean executives favour setting up facilities abroad. Malaysian and Filipino food executives are split between expanding present facilities or increasing the number of goods they now produce.

"Executives pick long-term bank loans and retained earnings as their top two choices to finance investments for the next five years," the NUS researchers said. Most of the investments will go into new machinery.
Wee said expansion "is a very strong indication of the very optimistic outlook" of the industry in Southeast Asia and India.

Visser urged governments around the region to pay more attention to the needs of food companies. Export growth in Southeast Asia has largely been driven by the strong sales of the electronic and semiconductor industries.
"Sometimes, they have a bit of feeling that governments are focusing too much on non-food industries and not on the food industries," he said.
Rabobank said in a study that India is on the way to becoming a major force in the global food market.

India is already the world's largest producer of sugar and tea and the second largest milk provider. It is also now one of the biggest growers of oilseeds, fruits and vegetables and a major producer of rice, wheat, groundnuts, coffee, tobacco, rubber, spices and potatoes, Rabobank said.
"The bright prospects for India will be enhanced by the GATT agreement, making Indian products far more competitive on the world market," Rabobank said.
The only hindrance to India's success is its rapidly growing population, which is approaching the one billion mark.
"Domestic tea consumption is already outstripping production rises, making it difficult to understand how the optimistic export prognoses will be met, the bank concluded.
